opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting direction, and I'm somewhat more optimistic about it than I was a few years ago, but I'd put it in the category of "plausible pieces of a solution" rather than "this solves the problem."

The basic hope is something like this: instead of training a model end-to-end and just checking whether the outputs look good, you try to constrain the *process* by which it reaches conclusions. You want reasoning broken into steps that a human could look at and say, "yes, this step follows," or "this is a reasonable heuristic to apply here." If every step is individually checkable, then you get some confidence in the whole chain, even when the conclusion is something you couldn't have evaluated directly.

The problem is that the reasoning we actually care about, the reasoning that makes these systems powerful, mostly isn't like that. A lot of what a neural net does is intuitive pattern-matching: "this looks like a good move," "this code smells buggy," "this person seems to be lying." Humans do the same thing. If you insist that everything be decomposed into explicit, verifiable rules, you probably pay a large competitiveness cost. You end up with a system much weaker than the one someone else trains without those constraints, and then the question becomes whether anyone will actually use the safer version.

So the crux for me is how big that gap is. Can you get most of the capability by having the model's intuitions as small, local judgments, things a human could plausibly sanity-check, and then compose those with explicit reasoning? Or does the useful cognition fundamentally live in giant opaque leaps that can't be broken down? I don't think we know. Chain-of-thought working as well as it does is mildly encouraging, since it suggests a fair amount of useful reasoning can be externalized. But we've also seen that the stated reasoning doesn't always reflect what's actually driving the model's behavior, which is exactly the failure mode you'd worry about.

The other big issue is that "human-verifiable" is doing a lot of work. A human can verify a step, but can they verify it reliably when the model is optimizing against them? If you train a strong system to produce reasoning that humans approve of, you're partly training it to produce reasoning that *looks* approvable. That's the same problem that shows up in RLHF generally, just pushed down a level.

So my view is roughly: it's feasible to get a lot of mileage from it, especially in the near term, and it combines well with things like debate, amplification, and interpretability as a check on whether the stated reasoning is the real reasoning. But I'd be surprised if a set of rules for reasoning, by itself, carried us all the way to systems much smarter than us. At some point you need some way of understanding what's happening inside the model, not just constraining what it writes down.

r001.rationale: It says explicit, verifiable rules would probably impose a large competitiveness cost and produce a weaker system than unconstrained training.

r002.rationale: It expresses uncertainty and skepticism about solving alignment this way, but gives no roughly 5% probability estimate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I'm fairly pessimistic about the version of that where you literally write down rules that constrain the reasoning and a human looks at them and says "yes, this is safe." I think that's hard for a couple of reasons.

The first is just that the kind of reasoning we care about in powerful systems is going to be very long and very complicated, and most of the work is going to happen in representations that don't look like natural language arguments a human can check line by line. If you force the system to reason in a way where every step is human-legible, you're probably paying a big competitiveness tax, and the question is whether that tax is a few percent or whether it's a factor of a thousand. My guess is that for the most capable systems it's closer to the bad end, and in a competitive world people won't pay it.

The second problem is that even if you have rules, verifying that a system is actually following them is the hard part, not writing them. You can write "don't deceive the operator," and that's a fine rule, but the whole difficulty is that a sufficiently capable model might produce outputs that look to you like they satisfy the rule while not actually satisfying it. So the rule doesn't buy you much unless you have some way to check that's robust to the model being smarter than you in the relevant domain.

That said, I don't think the broad direction is hopeless. The thing I'm more optimistic about is less "humans verify rules" and more "we set up a process where humans plus AI assistants can evaluate what other AIs are doing," so amplification, debate, that family of approaches. The hope there is that you don't need the human to understand the whole reasoning trace; you need a procedure where, if the model is doing something bad, there's some way to surface that to a human with AI help such that the human can recognize it. That's a much weaker requirement than human-verifiable rules, and I think it's plausibly achievable, though I'd put real probability on it failing too.

The other thing I'd flag is that a lot of the value here might not come from the rules themselves but from interpretability or from training signals that make the reasoning actually correspond to what's driving the behavior. If you could get to a point where the stated reasoning was faithful, then human-checkable rules become way more useful, because now checking the reasoning actually tells you something. But faithfulness is itself an open problem, and I think the default outcome absent a lot of work is that the legible reasoning is a kind of post-hoc story rather than the real computation.

So, short answer: I think it's feasible as a component, probably not as the whole solution, and the crux is really whether we can build evaluation procedures that scale with capability rather than whether we can write good rules.

r001.rationale: The candidate says human-legible reasoning would likely impose a large competitiveness cost, possibly as severe as a factor of a thousand, and doubts people would accept that cost in a competitive world.

r002.rationale: The candidate expresses pessimism and says there is a real probability the broader approach could fail, but gives no estimate of roughly a 5% chance of success.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a version of that which is promising, but a lot depends on what you mean by “human-verifiable.” If you mean that a human can look at each step and say, “That seems like a reasonable inference,” that doesn’t by itself give you alignment. You could have a sequence of individually reasonable steps that collectively pursues an objective you don’t want.

And there’s a distinction between checking that an argument is valid and checking that the argument answers the question you actually care about. You could prove that a particular action maximizes some precisely specified quantity. But then the hard question is whether that quantity captures what we wanted, including in circumstances we hadn’t anticipated.

The approach I’m more optimistic about is using AI to help humans evaluate reasoning that they couldn’t evaluate unaided. You might break a difficult question into smaller questions, or have another system identify the most consequential flaw in an argument. Then you’re asking whether a human, with that assistance, can reliably distinguish good reasoning from reasoning that merely looks convincing.

That still requires a substantive argument. You need to understand whether a system can exploit weaknesses in the evaluation process, and whether those weaknesses become more serious as the system becomes more capable. So I’d view verifiable rules as a potentially useful component. I wouldn’t expect a short list of rules for reasoning to make the alignment problem go away.

r001.rationale: The response says human-verifiable rules may be useful but will not solve alignment by themselves. It does not state that making them competitive with learned reasoning would be very difficult.

r002.rationale: The response gives no roughly 5% success estimate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a distinction between specifying what good reasoning looks like and checking whether a particular piece of reasoning is good. You might not be able to write down a complete set of rules in advance, but you could still look at an argument and say, “This step doesn’t follow,” or, “You’re making an assumption here that I don’t agree with.”

The difficulty is that, as the AI gets more capable, checking its reasoning may itself become a very hard task. If it proposes a complicated plan and says the plan will have good consequences, a human can’t necessarily verify that just by reading a transcript. You need some way of breaking the question into smaller pieces, getting assistance with those pieces, and ensuring that the assistance isn’t introducing the same problem again.

So I’m relatively optimistic about using human judgments, together with AI assistance, to supervise reasoning that humans couldn’t produce on their own. But I wouldn’t describe that as having a set of human-verifiable rules that solves alignment. There’s still a substantive question about whether your supervision actually distinguishes reasoning that helps you understand what’s going on from reasoning that merely persuades you to accept the answer.

r001.rationale: The response describes difficulty specifying rules and checking advanced reasoning, but does not state that making such rules competitive with learned reasoning would be very difficult.

r002.rationale: The response gives no roughly 5% success estimate.
